```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import (MSTL, HistoricAverage, Naive,
                                  RandomWalkWithDrift, SeasonalNaive)
from statsforecast.utils import ConformalIntervals
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from utilsforecast.losses import mase

from coursekit import datasets as D
from coursekit import plotting as P

P.use_course_style()

spine = D.spine()
H = 24
train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=H)

sf = StatsForecast(
    models=[HistoricAverage(), Naive(), SeasonalNaive(season_length=12),
            RandomWalkWithDrift()],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95], fitted=True)
fv = sf.forecast_fitted_values()

MODELS = ["HistoricAverage", "Naive", "SeasonalNaive", "RWD"]
LABELS = {"HistoricAverage": "Mean", "Naive": "Naive",
          "SeasonalNaive": "Seasonal naive", "RWD": "Drift"}

# --- Ch 5.7: the decomposition route, as a fifth model -------------------
sf_stl = StatsForecast(
    models=[MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift())],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc_stl = sf_stl.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])

_scored = (test.merge(fc[["unique_id", "ds", "SeasonalNaive"]], on=["unique_id", "ds"])
               .merge(fc_stl[["unique_id", "ds", "MSTL"]], on=["unique_id", "ds"]))
STL_MASE, SN_MASE = (
    float(mase(_scored, models=[m], seasonality=12, train_df=train)[m].iloc[0])
    for m in ("MSTL", "SeasonalNaive")
)

# --- the three ways to draw the same interval, on one holdout -------------
resid_sn = (fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]).dropna()

boot_paths = P.bootstrap_paths(train["y"], resid_sn, h=H, season_length=12,
                               n_paths=5000, seed=7)
boot_fan = P.paths_to_fan(fc["ds"], boot_paths, levels=(80, 95))

sf_conf = StatsForecast(
    models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12,
                          prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=H))],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc_conf = sf_conf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])


def coverage_80(lo, hi, y=test["y"].to_numpy()):
    return float(((y >= np.asarray(lo)) & (y <= np.asarray(hi))).mean())


# --- and over 8 rolling origins, where a coverage rate can actually be measured
def _cv_coverage_80(model):
    cv = StatsForecast(models=[model], freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1).cross_validation(
        df=spine, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=8, level=[80])
    lo, hi = cv["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], cv["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]
    return float(((cv["y"] >= lo) & (cv["y"] <= hi)).mean())


def _cv_coverage_80_bootstrap():
    sf_sn = StatsForecast(models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12)],
                          freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1)
    inside = []
    for w in range(8):
        end = len(spine) - (8 - w) * 12
        tr, te = spine.iloc[:end], spine.iloc[end:end + 12]
        sf_sn.forecast(df=tr, h=12, fitted=True)
        fvw = sf_sn.forecast_fitted_values()
        paths = P.bootstrap_paths(tr["y"], fvw["y"] - fvw["SeasonalNaive"], h=12,
                                  season_length=12, n_paths=5000, seed=7)
        f = P.paths_to_fan(te["ds"], paths, levels=(80,))
        y = te["y"].to_numpy()
        inside.append((y >= f["lo-80"].to_numpy()) & (y <= f["hi-80"].to_numpy()))
    return float(np.concatenate(inside).mean())


CV_COV = {
    "Gaussian": _cv_coverage_80(SeasonalNaive(season_length=12)),
    "bootstrap": _cv_coverage_80_bootstrap(),
    "conformal": _cv_coverage_80(SeasonalNaive(
        season_length=12,
        prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=12))),
}


def as_fan(model, frame=fc):
    return frame.rename(columns={
        model: "mean",
        f"{model}-lo-80": "lo-80", f"{model}-hi-80": "hi-80",
        f"{model}-lo-95": "lo-95", f"{model}-hi-95": "hi-95",
    })
```

## The Day 2 plan

Day 1 found the spine's signal is seasonality. Day 2 builds the floor a model must beat, and the way to prove a forecast is real.

::: {.incremental}
- **Four baseline models**, plus the decomposition route: the floor to beat
- **Residual diagnostics**: has the model taken all the signal?
- **Prediction intervals**: the Gaussian formula, and why it fails here
- **Two repairs**: resample the errors, then stop assuming a distribution
:::

A point forecast without an interval is an incomplete guess.

# A. The benchmark floor {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 5.1–5.2 · Simple, strong baselines

## Four benchmarks set the floor a model must clear

::: {.incremental}
- **Mean**: average of all historical observations
- **Naive**: last observed value ($\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_T$)
- **Seasonal Naive**: same season from previous year ($\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_{T+h-m}$)
- **Drift**: last value plus average historical trend slope
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Always fit these 4 first. On many series, **Seasonal Naive is tough to beat**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not let these sound like toys. On a seasonal series a seasonal naive is a
genuinely hard opponent, and by the end of today they will have watched it beat
a decomposition model over eight folds.

Worth saying which is which in plain language: the mean forgets time entirely,
the naive remembers only yesterday, the seasonal naive remembers this month last
year, and the drift draws a straight line through the first and last points. Ask
the room which one they expect to win here before you show them.
:::

## Only one benchmark has the shape of the data

```{python}
plt.show()
```

```python
sf = StatsForecast(freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1, models=[
    HistoricAverage(), Naive(), SeasonalNaive(season_length=12),
    RandomWalkWithDrift(),
])
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])

P.forecast_overlay(train, fc, MODELS, labels=LABELS, actual=test, history_tail=72)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Point at the flat pink line first. That is the mean model, and on a series that
has grown sixfold it is visibly hopeless - which is the point of showing it. The
green naive line is flat too, but at the right level.

The orange seasonal naive is the only one with the shape of the data in it. Let
the room see that before any number is quoted.
:::

## A benchmark is what turns a score into evidence

::: {.incremental}
- **Objective evidence**: proves the complex model adds value
- **Sanity check**: catches complex ML models losing to naive rules
- **Scale baseline**: provides a standard denominator for errors (MASE)
- **Fast**: takes just a few lines of code
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## The question to ask in every review
*"What is the simple baseline, and by how much did we beat it?"*
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to slow down on if the room is senior. The question in the
callout is the one to take back to work: it costs nothing to ask, and it is the
single most effective check on a forecasting claim.

The MASE point is worth a sentence now because the metric arrives in lecture 2:
the benchmark is not only a rival, it is also the denominator that makes errors
comparable across series.
:::

# B. Residuals {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 5.3–5.4 · Has the model finished?

## Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not

**Residual** ($e_t$): Error on *in-sample training data* (one-step ahead)

$$e_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}$$

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Two errors to keep straight
- **Residuals** = In-sample training errors (flattering)
- **Forecast Errors** = Out-of-sample holdout errors (honest)
:::

::: {.notes}
This distinction causes more confusion later than anything else in the day, so
make it concrete: a residual is what the model got wrong on data it had already
seen; a forecast error is what it got wrong on data it had not. Residuals
flatter, forecast errors do not.

Everything in segment B is residuals. Everything in lecture 2 is forecast
errors. Say that now and it saves a question later.
:::

## Two properties finish a model, two license its intervals

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Essential]{.card-title}

1. **Uncorrelated** ($r_k \approx 0$)  
   $\rightarrow$ No signal left behind
2. **Zero Mean** ($\bar{e} = 0$)  
   $\rightarrow$ Unbiased forecast
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[For Valid Intervals]{.card-title}

3. **Constant Variance**  
   $\rightarrow$ Homoscedastic
4. **Normally Distributed**  
   $\rightarrow$ Gaussian intervals valid
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The split matters: the first two are about whether the model is finished, and
the last two are about whether its intervals can be trusted. A model can pass
the left column and fail the right, and the intervals will still be wrong.

Segments C, D and E are, in order, the three ways to stop relying on the right
column.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8.6
resid = fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]
P.residual_diagnostics(resid, ds=fv["ds"], figsize=(8.6, 3.5),
                       title="Seasonal naive: residual diagnostics")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# fv = train merged with StatsForecast fitted values (sf.forecast(..., fitted=True))
resid = fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]
P.residual_diagnostics(resid, ds=fv["ds"])
```

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
r = resid.dropna()
print(f"mean residual {r.mean():+.2f}   "
      f"SD, first 10 years {r.head(120).std():.1f}   "
      f"SD, last 10 years {r.tail(120).std():.1f}")
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Zero mean** fails: the forecast is biased high by about 8 units
- **Constant variance** fails: the spread grows with the level
- **Uncorrelated** fails: ACF spikes stay outside the bounds, so signal is left
:::

::: {.notes}
Three panels, three verdicts. The time plot fans out - the spread in the 2010s
is roughly three times the spread in the 1980s, so constant variance fails. The
ACF has spikes well outside the bounds, so uncorrelated fails. The histogram is
sharply peaked with fat tails, so normal fails.

Do not treat that as a failure of the seasonal naive. It is the honest state of
the best benchmark on this series, and every interval method in this deck is a
response to one of those three lines.
:::

## Ljung-Box tests whether the autocorrelations are jointly zero

The first $\ell$ autocorrelations, tested jointly:

$$Q = T(T+2)\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}\frac{r_k^2}{T-k}$$

::: {.incremental}
- **Small $p$-value ($p < 0.05$)** $\rightarrow$ Significant autocorrelation $\rightarrow$ **Model incomplete**
- **Large $p$-value ($p \ge 0.05$)** $\rightarrow$ Residuals are indistinguishable from white noise
:::

```{python}
#| echo: true
r = resid.dropna()                      # no fitted value for the first m months
lb_p = acorr_ljungbox(r, lags=[24], return_df=True)["lb_pvalue"].iloc[0]
print(f"Seasonal naive residuals, {len(r)} obs, lag 24:  p = {lb_p:.1e}")
```

::: {.notes}
Rule of thumb: use lag l=10 for non-seasonal data, l=2m for seasonal data.
:::

# C. Prediction intervals {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

Ch 5.5 · Quantifying uncertainty

## A range is what a decision can act on

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Point forecast]{.card-title}

*"Demand will be 340 units."*

- Guaranteed to be wrong
- Hides the operational risk
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Interval forecast]{.card-title}

*"Demand: [300, 380], 80% of the time."*

- Sizes the safety stock
- States the risk out loud
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Decisions like staffing buffers, warehouse capacity, and safety inventory depend directly on the interval width.
:::

## One number becomes a range by adding uncertainty

Estimate the residual spread, then step out by a multiplier:

$$\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T - K - M}\sum_{t=1}^{T} e_t^2}
\qquad\qquad
\hat{y}_{T+1|T} \pm c\,\hat{\sigma}$$

::: {.incremental}
- $K$ = parameters estimated, $M$ = missing residuals (a seasonal naive has no fitted value for its first $m$ months)
- $c = 1.28$ for 80%, $c = 1.96$ for 95%
:::

::: {.notes}
Two things students trip on. The M term: a seasonal naive cannot produce a
fitted value for its first twelve months, so twelve residuals are missing and
the denominator has to know that. And c is a normal quantile - 1.28 and 1.96 are
only right if the residuals are normal, which we just showed they are not.

Flag that now. The rest of the deck is the repair.
:::

## How fast the range widens depends on the method

| Benchmark | $h$-step forecast standard deviation |
|---|---|
| Mean | $\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{1 + 1/T}$ |
| Naive | $\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h}$ |
| Seasonal naive | $\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{k+1}$, &nbsp; $k = \lfloor (h-1)/m \rfloor$ |
| Drift | $\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{T-1}\right)}$ |

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
## $\sqrt{h}$ is the *naive* case, not a law
For a **seasonal naive** the width is a **staircase**: flat inside a year, one
step up per complete year crossed. $k$ counts those years.
:::

::: {.notes}
All four formulas assume the residuals are uncorrelated. That assumption is
already known to be false here - segment B just rejected it at p ~ 1e-240.
:::

## The Gaussian interval rests on three assumptions

::: {.incremental}
1. Residuals are **uncorrelated**: otherwise $\hat{\sigma}$ understates the spread
2. Residuals have **constant variance**: one $\hat{\sigma}$ for the whole series
3. Residuals are **normally distributed**: otherwise $c = 1.28$ is the wrong multiplier
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
On this series **all three fail.** The next two methods each buy one of them back.
:::

::: {.notes}
Count them off on your fingers, because the next three segments buy them back
one at a time and it helps if the room is counting with you. Bootstrap buys back
normality. Conformal buys back the distribution entirely. Nothing in this course
buys back independence.
:::

## The spread grew eightfold and the tails are fat

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9.5
P.residual_assumption_plot(resid_sn, ds=fv["ds"], window=36, level=80,
                           figsize=(9.5, 3.1),
                           titles=("Rolling 3-year residual SD",
                                   "Central 80%: empirical (blue) vs normal (orange)"))
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: seasonal naive in-sample residuals on the spine (resid_sn)
r = resid_sn.to_numpy()

# Left  - constant variance? A 3-year rolling SD against the pooled sigma-hat.
pd.Series(r).rolling(36).std()

# Right - normal? Histogram against a normal of the SAME SD, plus the two
#         candidate 80% cut points.
np.quantile(r, [0.1, 0.9])                    # the bootstrap's cut points
1.2816 * r.std(ddof=1) * np.array([-1., 1.])  # the Gaussian's cut points
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- The rolling SD wanders between **4 and 35**: never the single 17.6 assumed
- Excess kurtosis **≈ 5.7**: sharper peak *and* fatter tails than a normal
:::

::: {.notes}
Left panel: a 36-month rolling standard deviation runs from about 4 in the
mid-1980s to about 34 at its peak, and the dashed line is the single pooled
sigma-hat of 17.6 that the closed-form interval uses for the whole series. One
number, for a spread that moved by a factor of eight.

Right panel: the blue lines are the empirical central 80%, the dashed orange are
where the normal assumption puts them. The normal cuts sit further out, which is
the tails being fat and the peak being sharp. The Gaussian interval is paying
for a shape the data does not have.
:::

# D. Bootstrapped intervals {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 5.5 · Dropping the normality assumption

::: {.notes}
Roughly 55 minutes in, and the real break is still 40 minutes away at the deck
boundary. Take two minutes here and let the room stand up. Segments D and E are
the densest stretch of Day 2, and they land better on a room that has moved.
:::

## Resample the errors you actually saw

A one-step error is $e_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}$. For the **naive** method
$\hat{y}_{t|t-1} = y_{t-1}$, so $y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t$, and a future value can be
*simulated* by drawing a past error:

$$y^*_{T+1} = y_T + e^*_{T+1}, \qquad
  y^*_{T+2} = y^*_{T+1} + e^*_{T+2}, \qquad \dots$$

. . .

For the **seasonal naive** the same recursion runs on the seasonal lag:

$$y^*_{T+i} = y^*_{T+i-m} + e^*_{T+i}$$

::: {.notes}
The star means "one possible future that could have occurred", not the observed
value. Run it 5000 times and you have 5000 possible futures.
:::

## The assumption you just made

::: {.cardbox .navy}
The simple residual bootstrap assumes the residuals come from **one common
distribution $\hat{F}$ whose distributional characteristics do not change over
time**: i.i.d. draws from the pool of past errors.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Bought:** normality. The interval is now whatever shape the errors are, and need not be symmetric.
- **Still owed:** independence, and *identical distribution*.
- On this series the second one is false: the residual SD tripled.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every interval method spends an assumption; the honest question is which one.
The bootstrap trades normality for identical distribution, and on this series
that trade is a bad one - the residual SD tripled, so 1980s errors are in the
same draw pool as 2010s errors.

That is not a reason to avoid the bootstrap. It is a reason to know which knob
you are turning, and the lab turns it: restricting the pool to recent residuals
moves coverage from about 62% to about 87%.
:::

## 5000 possible futures

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.sim_paths_plot(train, fc["ds"], boot_paths, n_show=8, history_tail=60,
                 actual=test, figsize=(10, 3.4),
                 title="Eight of the 5000 simulated sample paths")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover, seasonal naive residuals
resid_sn = (fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]).dropna()

boot_paths = P.bootstrap_paths(train["y"], resid_sn, h=24, season_length=12,
                               n_paths=5000, seed=7)     # -> (5000, 24)
P.sim_paths_plot(train, fc["ds"], boot_paths, n_show=8, actual=test)
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .teal}
The band is not the method. The **paths** are the method; the band is a
percentile taken down each column.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that fixes the most common misconception about the bootstrap.
Students see the shaded band and assume the band is the method. It is not. The
method is these paths; the band is a percentile taken down each column
afterwards.

Trace one path with your finger from the origin out to 24 months, and say: this
is one possible future, drawn by taking last year's value and adding a real
error we actually observed at some point in the past.
:::

## Bootstrap vs Gaussian on the spine

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.fan_chart_panels(train, [as_fan("SeasonalNaive"), boot_fan],
                   titles=("Gaussian, plus/minus c sigma-hat",
                           "Bootstrap, 5000 paths"),

plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# boot_fan = P.paths_to_fan(fc["ds"], boot_paths, levels=(80, 95))
#   -> ds / mean / lo-80 / hi-80 / lo-95 / hi-95, from empirical percentiles
P.fan_chart(train, as_fan("SeasonalNaive"), levels=(80, 95), actual=test)
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- Mean **80%** width: 59.7 Gaussian vs **46.4** bootstrap, a fifth narrower
- Mean **95%** width: 91.3 vs **90.1**, the gap has closed
- Sharp peak, fat tails. That is what excess kurtosis of 5.7 buys you
:::

::: {.notes}
Same model, same point forecast, same data. Only the assumption changed, and the
80% band got a fifth narrower.

Notice the 95% bands barely differ. That is the shape of the residuals showing
up exactly where you would expect it: the sharp peak makes the central 80%
tighter, and the fat tails put the 95% back where the normal had it.
:::

# E. Conformal prediction {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 5.5 · Distribution-free intervals, and the only method that
works on a model with no formula

## Name the error first: $e_{t+h|t}$

$$e_{t+h|t} = y_{t+h} - \hat{y}_{t+h|t}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $t$ | the time the forecast was **made**: the forecast origin |
| $h$ | the forecast **horizon** |
| $t+h$ | the future time being **predicted** |
| $y_{t+h}$ | what actually happened |
| $\hat{y}_{t+h\,\vert\,t}$ | the forecast made at time $t$ for time $t+h$ |

::: {.callout-note}
At $h = 1$ these are exactly the residuals from part B. For $h > 1$ they are a
different, wider set of errors, and they must be *collected*, not fitted.
:::

::: {.notes}
Notation discipline pays off here. e_{t+h|t} carries two indices for a reason:
which point is being forecast, and which origin it was forecast from. A 12-step
error made in 2010 and a 12-step error made in 2016 are two members of the same
calibration set.

Residuals had one index because there was only ever one origin: yesterday.
:::

## A worked example of $e_{t+h|t}$

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Walk-through
You hold $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{10}$ and want a **3-step-ahead** interval.

::: {.incremental}
1. Stand at $t = 5$. Pretend $y_6 \dots y_{10}$ do not exist yet.
2. Forecast three steps out: $\hat{y}_{8|5}$.
3. Now look up what really happened: $y_8$.
4. Record $e_{{8|5}} = y_8 - \hat{{y}}_{{8|5}}$, one 3-step-ahead error.
:::

. . .

Slide the origin to $t = 6, 7, \dots$ and repeat. What you collect is the
**calibration set** for $h = 3$.

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
toy = pd.DataFrame({"ds": np.arange(1, 11),
                    "y": [10., 12, 11, 14, 13, 16, 15, 18, 17, 20]})
toy_err = pd.DataFrame([
    {"cutoff": t, "ds": t + 3,
     "y": toy["y"].iloc[t + 2],       # y_{t+3}
     "yhat": toy["y"].iloc[t - 1]}    # naive: y-hat_{t+3|t} = y_t
    for t in (5, 6, 7)
])
P.h_step_error_diagram(toy, toy_err, figsize=(9, 3.9), xticks=range(1, 11),
                       title="Three 3-step-ahead errors, from three origins")
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Walk this by hand on the numbers. Stand at t=5, the naive forecast for t=8 is
whatever y_5 was, then look up what actually happened at t=8 and subtract.
That single number is one member of the calibration set.

Slide the origin forward and you get another. Conformal prediction is nothing
more elaborate than collecting those and taking a quantile of their absolute
values.
:::

## Exchangeability, not i.i.d.

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Conformal prediction replaces i.i.d. with **exchangeability**: the past
$h$-step errors carry no information in their *order*.
:::

. . .

The interval is then an empirical quantile of the collected errors:

$$\hat{y}_{T+h|T} \pm Q_{1-\alpha}\!\left(\left|e_{t+h|t}\right|\right)$$

::: {.incremental}
- One quantile **per horizon $h$**: widening with $h$ is *measured*, not assumed
- No $\hat{\sigma}$, no $c$, no assumed distribution: hence *distribution-free*
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that earns the segment, so do not rush it.

Exchangeability is weaker than i.i.d., and the difference is worth spelling out.
I.i.d. says every error is an independent draw from one fixed distribution.
Exchangeability says only this: if you shuffled the order of the errors you
collected, you would not be able to tell. That permits dependence i.i.d.
forbids, which matters here, because the bootstrap's i.i.d. assumption is the
one this series breaks.

Then the payoff. Because the interval is an empirical quantile of errors the
model actually made, there is no sigma-hat to estimate and no c to look up, and
nothing anywhere assumes a shape. That is why this method works on a model whose
interval has no formula, which is most of what Day 3 covers.
:::

## Where the calibration set comes from

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
cs = sf.cross_validation(df=train, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=4)
cs12 = (cs[cs["ds"] == cs["cutoff"] + pd.DateOffset(months=12)]
        .rename(columns={"SeasonalNaive": "yhat"})[["cutoff", "ds", "y", "yhat"]])
P.h_step_error_diagram(train.tail(84), cs12, figsize=(10, 4.2),
                       title="Four origins, h = 12: the errors conformal quantifies")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Roll the origin backwards; keep the error at the horizon you care about.
cs = sf.cross_validation(df=train, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=4)
cs12 = (cs[cs["ds"] == cs["cutoff"] + pd.DateOffset(months=12)]
        .rename(columns={"SeasonalNaive": "yhat"})[["cutoff", "ds", "y", "yhat"]])
P.h_step_error_diagram(train.tail(84), cs12)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
statsforecast does exactly this internally: n_windows rolling origins, the
absolute error at each horizon, then the empirical quantile of those.
:::

## Any model at all can be given a conformal interval

```python
from statsforecast.utils import ConformalIntervals

sf_conf = StatsForecast(
    models=[SeasonalNaive(
        season_length=12,
        prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=24),
    )],
    freq="MS",
)
fc_conf = sf_conf.forecast(df=train, h=24, level=[80, 95])
```

::: {.incremental}
- `n_windows`: how many rolling origins make up the calibration set
- Needs at least $2h + 1$ observations; more windows, steadier quantiles
- With 8 windows only 16 scores sit behind each horizon, so the band is **visibly jittery**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the practical payoff of the whole segment and the thing a Day 3 author
will need: any model that has no closed-form interval gets one from
prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(...). Not every statsforecast model can
produce intervals on its own; all of them can produce conformal ones.

The jitter warning is worth making concrete. With eight windows there are only
sixteen scores behind each horizon, so the band wobbles. That is a small sample
showing through, not a bug.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = []
for lab, lo, hi in [
    ("Gaussian", fc["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
    ("Bootstrap", boot_fan["lo-80"], boot_fan["hi-80"]),
    ("Conformal", fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
]:
    rows.append({"method": lab,
                 "mean 80% width": float(np.mean(np.asarray(hi) - np.asarray(lo))),
                 "coverage (24 pts)": coverage_80(lo, hi)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False,
      formatters={"mean 80% width": "{:.1f}".format,
                  "coverage (24 pts)": "{:.0%}".format}))
```

::: {.notes}
One point forecast, three bands. Left panel says they are not the same object;
right panel says how they differ in shape. Gaussian is the staircase, bootstrap
is narrow, conformal is jittery.

The printed numbers are the trap, so read them out and then say plainly where
they came from: 24 points. The next slide is the arithmetic on why that cannot
separate three methods.
:::

## Each method buys back a different assumption

| Method | Assumes | Buys you |
|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | uncorrelated · constant variance · **normal** | a closed form, one line of code |
| Bootstrap | uncorrelated · **i.i.d. from $\hat{F}$** | asymmetry, any error shape |
| Conformal | **exchangeable** $h$-step errors | no assumed distribution at all |

::: {.callout-important}
Pick by which assumption you can defend, not by the widths on the last slide.
:::

::: {.notes}
The table is the takeaway. Each row is a trade, and the honest question when
choosing is not "which is most accurate" but "which of these three assumptions
am I willing to make about this series".

If the room wants a default: conformal, because it assumes least, and because it
is the one that generalises to models that have no formula. That is also why it
is the one Day 3 will lean on.
:::

## Why one test window is misleading

On a single small test set ($n = 24$), coverage error is large:

$$\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.8 \times 0.2}{24}} \approx \pm 8\% \quad (\pm 16\% \text{ at } 95\% \text{ CI})$$

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
A nominal 80% interval could easily measure anywhere from **64% to 96%** on a
single 24-point holdout by chance alone.
:::

. . .

Over **8 rolling origins** (96 scored points) they separate cleanly:

```{python}
#| echo: false
print("80% coverage over 96 scored points:   "
      + "   ".join(f"{k} {v:.0%}" for k, v in CV_COV.items()))
```

::: {.notes}
The bootstrap's 61% is the identically-distributed assumption being punished:
pooling 1980s residuals (SD about 8) with 2010s residuals (SD 25) makes the draw pool
far too tight for a forecast issued in 2016. Restricting the pool to the last
120 residuals takes it to about 87%; the last 60 push it to 91%. The assumption is the knob, and the lab turns it.
:::
